summary: Specifies two variants of the two-message issuance protocol for Privacy Pass tokens. One produces tokens that are privately verifiable with the issuer's private key; the other produces tokens that are publicly verifiable with the issuer's public key.

eli5.summary: This explains how a ticket booth hands out anonymous tickets. In one version only the booth can check them, and in the other anyone can.

questions: what is a privacy pass token request
subtitle: How a client gets an anonymous Privacy Pass token from an issuer in a single request and response.

tldr.problem: Privacy Pass lets a client prove it was approved by a server in the past without revealing which request it is. That needs a concrete protocol for the issuer to hand out tokens that it cannot later link back to the client.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends one TokenRequest over HTTP POST containing a blinded value, and the issuer answers with one TokenResponse. The client unblinds the result into a token. Two variants exist: an OPRF-based one that only the issuer can verify, and a blind RSA one that anyone with the issuer public key can verify.
tldr.outcome: The RFC registers token types 0x0001 (VOPRF, privately verifiable) and 0x0002 (Blind RSA, publicly verifiable), plus the media types and well-known URI used to run issuance.

today: RFC 9578 is a Proposed Standard and, per the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It is the specification of the two Privacy Pass issuance protocols, used together with RFC 9576 and RFC 9577.

sections.title: What the Issuance Protocols Do
sections.content:
The Privacy Pass protocol is a privacy-preserving authorization mechanism. A Client can present cryptographic tokens that prove nothing other than that a given server created them in the past. The overall design is covered in RFC 9576; this document covers only how tokens are issued.

It defines two issuance protocols, each built on HTTP (RFC 9110). One produces tokens that are privately verifiable with the Issuer Private Key and is based on an Oblivious Pseudorandom Function (OPRF, RFC 9497). The other produces tokens that are publicly verifiable with the Issuer Public Key and is based on the blind RSA signature scheme (RFC 9474).

The RFC does not cover the Privacy Pass architecture, the deployment choices, or the application-specific choices for protecting Client privacy. Those are left to RFC 9576.
sections.eli5: This RFC is the part of Privacy Pass about handing out the tickets. It describes two kinds of tickets, one that only the booth can check and one that anyone can check.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
The Client receives a TokenChallenge from the redemption protocol (RFC 9577) and uses an issuance protocol to produce the matching token. Issuance is a one-round exchange: a TokenRequest from the Client and a TokenResponse from the Issuer.

The challenge can be interactive or non-interactive and can be per Origin or across Origins. The details of attestation, meaning how the Client convinces the Issuer side that it deserves a token, are outside the scope of the issuance protocol. The protocols work with any deployment model defined in RFC 9576.
sections.eli5: You get a challenge from a website, you send a sealed request to the booth, the booth sends back a sealed answer, and you open it to get your ticket.

sections.title: Issuer Configuration and the Directory
sections.content:
An Issuer MUST provide two parameters: an Issuer Request URL where token requests are sent, and a list of Issuer Public Key values. They are published in a JSON directory object with the fields issuer-request-uri and token-keys. Each entry in token-keys has a token-type integer and a token-key, the base64url-encoded public key including padding.

An entry may also carry an optional not-before UNIX timestamp to help with scheduled key rotation. Clients SHOULD NOT use a key before that time, and SHOULD use the first key in the list that has no not-before value or has one in the past. Issuers can advertise several keys for the same token type, with earlier keys preferred. Origins can try each key in turn when verifying, which helps with Client clock skew.

The directory has the media type application/private-token-issuer-directory and lives at /.well-known/private-token-issuer-directory. The directory and the Issuer resources SHOULD be on the same Origin. Issuers SHOULD allow caching with HTTP cache directives, and regular key rotation is recommended to limit the damage from a key compromise.
sections.eli5: The booth posts a sign at a well-known spot listing where to send requests and which stamps it uses. It can announce new stamps ahead of time, so everyone switches at the right moment.

sections.title: Privately Verifiable Tokens (Type 0x0001)
sections.content:
This variant is based on a verifiable OPRF using the P-384 curve and SHA-384. The Client creates a random 32-byte nonce, hashes the challenge with SHA-256 to get challenge_digest, and builds a token_input from the token type, nonce, digest and key identifier. It then blinds that input, so the Issuer sees only a blinded value.

The TokenRequest holds token_type (0x0001), a truncated_token_key_id and the blinded_msg. The truncated key ID is only the last byte of the full key ID, so an Issuer cannot use it to single out a Client. The request is an HTTP POST with media type application/private-token-request.

The Issuer checks that the token type is supported, that the truncated key ID matches one of its keys and that the blinded message has the right size. If any check fails, or the blinded element cannot be deserialized, it MUST return HTTP 422. Otherwise it evaluates the blinded element with its private key and returns a TokenResponse with the evaluated message and a proof, as application/private-token-response.

The Client verifies the proof and finalizes the result into an authenticator, producing a Token. To verify a token later, the Issuer recomputes the authenticator from the token contents using its private key and compares it with the one in the token. Only the holder of the private key can do this. Issuer keys MUST NOT be reused in other protocols.
sections.eli5: You put your ticket in a sealed envelope and the booth stamps it through the envelope. You open the envelope and keep the stamped ticket. Later, only the booth can tell the stamp is real.

sections.title: Publicly Verifiable Tokens (Type 0x0002)
sections.content:
This variant uses blind RSA signatures, specifically the RSABSSA-SHA384-PSS-Deterministic and RSABSSA-SHA384-PSSZERO-Deterministic variants from RFC 9474. The exchange has the same shape as the first variant: a random 32-byte nonce, a SHA-256 digest of the challenge, a blinded message in a TokenRequest with token_type 0x0002, and a TokenResponse carrying the blind signature.

The key difference is that anyone holding the Issuer Public Key can verify the token. The RFC points out that this means any Origin can choose a given Issuer without explicit coordination or permission, because the Issuer does not learn which Origin asked for the token.

Verification checks that the authenticator is a valid RSASSA-PSS signature over the rest of the token, using SHA-384, MGF1 with SHA-384, and a 48-byte salt. The key identifier is the SHA-256 hash of a DER-encoded SubjectPublicKeyInfo object. That object MUST use the RSASSA-PSS object identifier and MUST include the hash, mask generation and salt length parameters.

As in the first variant, Issuers SHOULD make sure the truncated forms of new key IDs do not collide with other keys in rotation. A collision can make the Issuer use the wrong private key, which makes the resulting tokens invalid, though the RFC says there is no known security consequence.
sections.eli5: It is the same sealed-envelope trick, but the stamp is one that anyone can check with the booth's public stamp pattern. A shop does not have to ask the booth first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This RFC only instantiates the issuance protocol on top of the VOPRF and blind RSA documents, so all security considerations from those documents also apply. Wider privacy and security concerns for multi-Client and multi-Issuer settings are covered in RFC 9576, including the privacy effects of the deployment models.

The notable considerations named are Issuer Public Key rotation and consistency, and Issuer selection. The truncated key ID in each request exists so that Issuers cannot use the key identifier as a way of uniquely identifying Clients.
sections.eli5: The booth must not be able to tell customers apart, so the request only carries a tiny piece of the key label. The rest of the safety advice lives in the big architecture document.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the well-known URI suffix private-token-issuer-directory and two entries in the Privacy Pass Token Types registry. Type 0x0001 is VOPRF(P-384, SHA-384), not publicly verifiable, with Nk of 48. Type 0x0002 is Blind RSA (2048-bit), publicly verifiable, with Nk of 256. Both have Nid of 32, and neither supports public or private metadata.

Three media types were also added: application/private-token-issuer-directory, application/private-token-request and application/private-token-response. The appendix of the RFC gives test vectors for both issuance protocols.
sections.eli5: The official list of token kinds and file labels got new entries, so everybody uses the same names for the two kinds of ticket.
